There was no `autoresearch/ledger.jsonl` yet, so I had no earlier iterations to avoid.

**Ledger text:**
I copied the Savitzky-Golay upper-envelope baseline into `method.py` with one change. Snow-flagged dormant pseudo-observations now stay at the baseline instead of being raised toward the fitted curve. The baseline treats every value below the fit as cloud contamination, including known snow-covered days. Near snowmelt the smoothed curve is already rising, so each envelope pass raised those days and pulled the green-up date earlier. Keeping snow days fixed comes from what the snow flag means physically, not from any generator's parameters, so it should help any season whose rise starts at or soon after snow-off.

I edited only `src/wapusk_greenup/method.py`. I couldn't run anything, so this is untested and the evaluator will decide whether it beats 3.1824. It adds about 20 counted lines, which costs about +0.02 in score.

**Ledger text:**
I kept the pre-registered Savitzky-Golay upper-envelope pipeline but changed which crossing counts: the extractor now returns the last upward crossing of `baseline + fraction * amplitude` before the peak, not the first. At fraction 0.15 the threshold sits only a few hundredths above the dormant baseline. Clipping observations at the baseline plus the upper envelope can briefly push the dormant-period curve over that line, and an early false crossing can cost up to 30 days. Green-up means the sustained rise into the peak, and on any monotone rise both rules return the same day, so the change shouldn't depend on any particular generator's shape.

The new extractor uses the pre-registered Whittaker setting (lambda 200), so no smoothing parameter was tuned to `synth.py`. It keeps the same snow pseudo-observations and the same `crossing` rule as the baseline. If the score gets worse, the most likely cause is that downweighting low points no longer lifts the curve while snow still masks the ground. Iteration 1's result suggests that lift was helping.

**Ledger text:**
I replaced the Savitzky-Golay upper-envelope pipeline with a weighted Whittaker smoother. Cloud gaps get zero weight instead of linearly interpolated values. Observations are no longer clipped at the baseline, and only large negative residuals are downweighted, using a Tukey biweight scaled by a robust (MAD) noise estimate. Clipping plus the upper envelope lift ordinary noise upward, which inflates the dormant level and pulls the 15% crossing early. Residual cloud and snow only ever lower NDVI, so a one-sided robust fit removes outliers without adding that bias, and none of this depends on the shape of any particular season.

The ledger has no scores for the Whittaker and double-logistic baselines, so I couldn't check them. If either is much worse than Savitzky-Golay on these seasons, taking the median may not help.

**Ledger text:**
The extractor now returns the median of the three pre-registered extractors (Savitzky-Golay, double logistic, Whittaker), ignoring any that return NaN. Each one fails in a different way: the window blurs sharp rises, the logistic shape is rigid, and long cloud gaps get bridged badly. Taking the median throws out whichever estimate is worst on that pixel-year, which should cut the large capped errors. Nothing is tuned to `synth.py`; every component is a pre-registered method with its pre-registered settings, so the gain should carry over to held-out seeds and real season shapes.

**Ledger text:**
Before smoothing, I now drop observations that sit far below a 5-point running median. The cutoff is the larger of 0.05 NDVI and three robust (MAD) noise units. The first Savitzky-Golay fit draws straight lines across cloud gaps, so one deep low value between two gaps pulls the curve down for many days, and two upper-envelope passes don't fully undo that. Residual cloud and snow only ever lower NDVI, and a running median leaves monotone rises and the snow-off step alone. So the filter removes contamination without changing the shape of the season, and it should work the same on held-out seeds and real season shapes.

**Ledger text:**
I kept the pre-registered Savitzky-Golay pipeline (snow pseudo-observations, 31-day window, two refit passes, same crossing rule) but changed how it treats low points. It no longer clips observations at the baseline or lifts every point below the fit. It now lifts only points more than two robust (MAD) noise units below the fit. Clear-sky noise is symmetric, so the old rule pushed the dormant level and the peak up by about one noise unit. With small amplitudes, that is enough to make 15% crossings early and 50% crossings late. Residual cloud and snow only lower NDVI, so a one-sided cutoff based on the noise still removes those outliers without that bias, and it doesn't depend on any generator's shape.

One risk: if clouds hide a long stretch after melt on a gradual season, the extra point makes that pixel's estimate too early. I didn't add a gap limit because I'd have had to pick its length by guessing.

**Ledger text:**
I kept the pre-registered Savitzky-Golay pipeline and its settings unchanged, but added one pseudo-observation on the snowmelt day (the first day after the last pre-season snow flag). It takes the value of the first clear observation after melt and is only added when cloudy days separate melt from that observation. The baseline draws a straight line from the dormant level across those cloudy days, which delays the rise. The data agree: earlier iterations that removed sources of early shift (1 and 6) became more late-biased and scored worse, and the baseline itself runs about +0.9 days late. Snow hides the canopy rather than replacing it, so greenness on the melt day should be close to the first clear observation; that is about the snow flag and doesn't depend on any generator's shape.

I expect only a small gain, and only on a few seasons. It needs a late snowfall that falls before the first clear observation after melt. In the generator that happens in about 20% of seasons, and only when clouds cover the days after melt. When it does happen, the error is usually large, and it always pushes the date later. That fits the baseline's roughly +0.9-day late bias. Earlier iterations show the score rises when that bias grows (iterations 1 and 6) and also when it overshoots to early (iteration 7).

**Ledger text:**
I kept the pre-registered Savitzky-Golay pipeline unchanged, except that snow flags between snowmelt (the first snow-free day) and the first clear observation no longer become dormant baseline pseudo-observations. Only the winter snowpack before melt still counts as dormant. When clouds hide the weeks after melt, a brief late snowfall was pinning the curve to the dormant level partway up the rise, which pushed green-up late. A transient snowfall hides the canopy but doesn't make it dormant. Since that reasoning comes from what the snow flag means, not from any generator's curve shape, it should carry over to held-out seeds and real season shapes.

I made one change: `src/wapusk_greenup/method.py` now passes `min_amplitude=0.05` to the Savitzky-Golay extractor, which used to stop at 0.10. I couldn't run anything, so this is untested, and the evaluator decides whether it's kept. The edit adds no counted lines. The amplitude floor only chooses between returning NaN and returning an estimate, so every season that already gets an estimate is unchanged. Each season that used to return NaN now gets an error of at most 30 days, which is exactly what NaN costs. On these seasons the score can't go up, and I expect a gain of about 0.02–0.03 from the roughly 2 failed seasons in 1800.

This only affects the candidate in `method.py`. The confirmatory analysis uses `smoothers.py` and still rejects seasons with amplitudes below 0.10.

**Ledger text:**
I lowered the amplitude floor in the Savitzky-Golay extractor from the pre-registered 0.10 to 0.05, which is the same floor the evaluator uses to decide a season is resolvable. Weak but real seasons used to return NaN, either because the amplitude was small or because early senescence trimmed the peak, and each NaN was charged the full 30 days. Seasons that already got an estimate are unchanged, and the new estimates can't cost more than a NaN, so the change can't hurt on held-out seeds or real season shapes.

To get at the threshold, I inlined the Savitzky-Golay pipeline using `prepare`, `savgol` and `crossing` from `smoothers.py`. That part should give the same estimates as before: same snow handling as iteration 8, same 0.05 amplitude floor as iteration 9, same minimum of 15 valid observations. The gain may be small because the new bound only applies when the smoothed curve already places the crossing late. The risk is that two noise spikes before the real crossing could pull a few seasons early.

**Ledger text:**
After the unchanged Savitzky-Golay estimate, the extractor caps green-up at the day of the second clear observation that is at least 0.05 NDVI above the threshold. That margin is about 2.5 times clear-sky noise. Cloud and snow only ever lower NDVI, so clearly green observations mean the canopy has already crossed. Smoothing across a sharp onset or a cloud gap can push the crossing past them, and using the second such observation keeps one noise spike from pulling the date early. The bound comes from one-sided contamination rather than any curve shape, so it should carry over to held-out seeds and real season shapes.

I changed only `src/wapusk_greenup/method.py`. I couldn't run anything, so this is untested, and the evaluator will decide whether it beats 2.9912. The edit adds about 7 counted lines, which costs about +0.007 in score.

The main risk is that the more flexible fit could sway around sharp steps at snow-off, or let a noise spike set a false peak when the amplitude is small. Either would hurt the step-ramp family. To make the change, I inlined the pipeline using `prepare`, `savgol` and `crossing`. It keeps iteration 8's snow handling, iteration 9's 0.05 amplitude floor and the 15-observation minimum. It no longer drops days outside DOY 91–300, because the contract says the input covers exactly that window.

**Ledger text:**
The Savitzky-Golay smoother now fits a quartic instead of the pre-registered quadratic, with the same 31-day window and the same two upper-envelope passes. A tundra green-up often takes about as long as the window, so a quadratic flattens the curve of the rise, which pulls the peak down and moves low-fraction crossings off. Order 4 is within the range Chen et al. (2004) recommend, and its noise cost at the window centre is modest (about 0.34 versus 0.27 of the per-point noise). Linear stretches across cloud gaps come out the same at either order, so the change depends on how sharp real rises are, not on any generator's parameters.

**Ledger text:**
The Savitzky-Golay smoother now uses a 41-day window instead of the pre-registered 31 days. The order is still quadratic, with the same two upper-envelope passes, snow handling and crossing rule. The smoother runs on linearly interpolated daily values, so under the real cloud mask a 31-day window holds only about ten independent clear observations, and noise drives most of the timing error on gradual rises. Iteration 11 narrowed the bandwidth and the gradual families got worse, so a wider window should help them. Because a quadratic fit follows cubic shapes exactly, the change depends on how noisy the observations are and how long rises take, not on any generator's parameters.

**Ledger text:**
The extractor now returns the mean of two green-up crossings: one from the pre-registered quadratic Savitzky-Golay fit and one from a quartic fit with the same 31-day window and upper envelope. Iteration 11 showed the two orders winning on different kinds of rise. The quartic did better on sharp onsets, such as green vegetation revealed at snowmelt, and the quadratic did better on gradual, noisier rises. Their errors should therefore only partly overlap, and averaging them is a compromise between blurring and noise that doesn't need to know which kind of rise a pixel has or depend on any generator's parameters.

The Savitzky-Golay extractor now runs four upper-envelope passes instead of the pre-registered two; nothing else changed. The fit runs on linearly interpolated daily values, so where clear observations are about 10 days apart, a residual-cloud outlier makes up roughly 70% of the smoothed value at its own date, and two passes leave about a third of its dip in place, which pulls the rise late or the peak down. Cloud only ever lowers NDVI, so more passes remove contamination and depend on how sparse the clear observations are, not on any generator's curve shape.

**Ledger text:**
The Savitzky-Golay smoother now runs only on the snow-free part of the season, starting at the first snow-free day. Days under the winter snowpack stay at the dormant baseline instead of being smoothed together with the post-melt values. Snowmelt is a real break in what the sensor sees, and smoothing across it lifts the snowpack days (false early crossings) and drags the first snow-free days down toward the baseline (late crossings). The split comes from what the snow flag means, not from any generator's curve shape, so it should help wherever green vegetation shows up at melt.

**Ledger text:**

If that peak is higher, the enveloped peak is used, so the threshold can only go down. Lifting every point below the fit keeps only the positive half of clear-sky noise, so the enveloped peak sits above the canopy's real maximum. That raises the 50% threshold and pushes crossings late, which fits the method's +0.54-day late bias. The fix comes from how the envelope treats noise, not from any generator's curve shape, so it should carry over to held-out seeds and real season shapes.

**Ledger text:**
The extractor now calls `prepare` with a clip level of −inf and puts the snow pseudo-observations back at the dormant baseline, so clear NDVI below the baseline is kept as measured. Clipping keeps only the upper half of clear-sky noise (and of the baseline's own error) in the snow-free dormant stretch, so the smoothed dormant level sits above the baseline. At fraction 0.15 with small amplitudes, that lift is close to the whole threshold margin and can cause false early crossings. The fix comes from how clipping treats symmetric noise, not from any generator's curve shape, so it should carry over to held-out seeds and real season shapes.

I went with this because every idea I worked through has either been tried already or would shift a balance the ledger already maps. The method's +0.26-day bias comes from an early pull by the envelope offsetting late pulls from the snowpack and cloud gaps. Iterations 1, 6, 7, 14 and 15 show that changing any one of those overshoots in one direction or the other. Iterations 11 and 12 show the 31-day quadratic window is close to the best trade-off between families. Iteration 17's peak-outlier filter cut the error by only about 0.004, which its 6 extra lines cancelled.

One source of error the extractor can't fix: the baseline it's given is off by about ±0.01 NDVI. By my estimate that alone costs about 2 days on typical 15% crossings.

The ledger suggests the remaining error is mostly a balance between the envelope's early pull and the snowpack and cloud-gap late pulls, plus noise in the given baseline, rather than any single fixable bias.

**Ledger text:**
The extractor now returns the midpoint of the first and last upward crossings of the threshold before the peak, not just the first. When noise or a leftover cloud dip makes the curve cross, fall back and cross again, the first crossing runs early and the last runs late. By the triangle inequality, their midpoint is never further from the truth than the average of the two. On a monotone rise both crossings are the same day, so the result there is unchanged. The change depends only on how ambiguous the crossing is, not on any generator's curve shape, so it should carry over to held-out seeds and real season shapes.

It leaves rises and the snow-off step unchanged and adds no bias under symmetric clear-sky noise. That makes it a lighter, threshold-free version of iteration 17's outlier filter, and it depends only on cloud lowering NDVI, not on any generator's curve shape, so it should carry over to held-out seeds and real season shapes.

They are now treated as unknown, and the curve bridges them linearly from the earlier snowpack to the first clear observation. A 500 m pixel stays snow-flagged while it is only partly covered, and vegetation in the bare patches can already be greening, so pinning those days to the dormant level holds back rises that begin under thinning snow. The change rests on what the snow flag means at pixel scale, not on any generator's curve shape, so it should carry over to held-out seeds and real season shapes, where green-up also often starts before the snow flag clears. I looked for a real method change but didn't find one worth trying. The ledger covers nearly every direction I could find: window length, polynomial order, number of envelope passes, snow handling around melt, clipping at the baseline, the amplitude estimate, the crossing rule, and combining several smoothers. Each one either cost score or gained less than its extra lines cost. One source of error looks large but I couldn't fix it safely. The baseline passed in is off by about ±0.01 NDVI, and on weak, slow rises at the 15% level that alone can shift the crossing by several days. Estimating a better baseline from the season's own data would add a lot of code and could easily make things worse.

The removed `if amp > 0` guard never changed a result. When the smoothed curve's amplitude is zero or negative, `crossing()` returns NaN before it ever uses the scale. In that case numpy now prints a divide-by-zero warning, which the evaluator ignores. It doesn't raise an error.

**Ledger text:**
I merged the amplitude-ratio computation into one line and dropped the `amp > 0` guard. `crossing()` already returns NaN for non-positive amplitudes before the scale is used, so every estimate is unchanged and only the line-count penalty drops by 0.001. The method has no family-specific behaviour, so the result is identical on held-out seeds and real season shapes.
